[The *Rāgapaṭamañjarī* of Luipāda: O tree of desire, all five branches are trembling; look at the flickering flame of time!
Firmly establish the measure of great bliss; Luī says, "Know it by asking the Guru."
Stanza: What is the use of all this mental composure? One dies regardless of whether it be happiness or suffering.
Dhruva: O Chandaka, you have bound me with the snare of deceit; come now, seize me by the neck!
Lui says: We saw them in meditation; both vomiting and belching, they sat there like two paṇḍits.
Dhruva: The body is the excellent tree; all five branches have been entered by Time, who is fickle-minded. ||1||
Having taken hold of Hara, experience great bliss; he who speaks thus, ask the Guru and understand.
What is achieved by all these meditative absorptions? One certainly dies because of pleasure and pain. ||2||
Having abandoned the binding of desires and the hope for deceit, and having attached yourself to the side of emptiness, O friend, obtain [or: cast off] its snare! 3.
Lūyī said: "I saw this in meditation while seated upon the two [peaks of] Dhavana and Cavana. ||4||

With my heart and intellect illuminated by tasting the nectar from the lotus-like mouth of the glorious true Guru, and with a face made serene through faith, I shall clearly compose a commentary in pure language upon this collection of most wondrous practices composed by the Siddhas, such as Śrī Uḍḍīśa and others, for the sake of attaining the realization of the non-dual wisdom of the glorious Kuliśeśvara.

[1] A multitude of drops of nectar from the lotus feet of the glorious Guru; the *Rāgapaṭamañjarī*: "The tree of the body," and so forth. With a heart made motionless by the intense bliss of being thoroughly satiated, the Siddhācārya Śrī Lūyīpāda—desiring to rescue those helpless and wretched people who were submerged in the middle of the ocean of delusion regarding the great duality of truth—spoke the words beginning with "the body" in the common vernacular (*prākṛta*) in order to compose a pedestal for pure reality (*śuddhadharmatā-pīṭhikā*) under the guise of the "tree of the body," impelled by his vow (*praṇidhi*).

The five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*), are the [constituents]. The six sense-faculties, the elements, and the objects are taken as the "excellent tree" because they possess the nature of sprouts characterized by the primary grasper, the grasping, and the perceived. Now, one might ask: since it is insentient, how can the body be an excellent tree? This is not a fault. For in the same way, even the authors of external treatises who are devoted to the ornament of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā-alaṅkāra*) have declared that similarity is based on some degree of difference. How much more so in this case, where, due to the defect of appearing as a natural state and through its flickering nature, Rāhu—being of a common (material) essence—is indeed of the nature of non-departure (*acyuti*).

That very time has arrived; the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapratipad) has entered. For, by the sequence of the lunar days—Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—the moon of the conventional bodhicitta is brought to desiccation. This [time] has been described in extreme terms as "black" by the venerable Āryapāda in the *Caryāgītikoṣa*: "If the fire of time enters, even the entire mountain, the cave, and the deep valley are destroyed; the pure water goes to exhaustion."
And thus, when the bodhicitta—the treasury of all accomplishments—has fallen into the mire of passion, and the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be blameless accomplishment?

And likewise, in the *Bhavatantrarāja* from the *Saṃpuṭa*: "The Vajrī has indeed described the mind as saṃsāra—that which is embodied by the darkness of manifold conceptualizations, flickering like a wind-driven and intoxicated lightning flash, and smeared with the stains of passion and other irresistible defilements."

Therefore, whoever among those with limited scope have fully ripened their wholesome roots, and who—preceded by the retention of the Blessed One’s means for entering the five stages—constantly seek the fruit of innate bliss in the form of the unified pair (*yuganaddha*), they too directly realize the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).

The venerable Āryadeva also said: "Without the sequence of the five stages (*pañcakrama*), the realization of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) cannot be attained. [This refers to the sequence beginning with] faith, etc. By this, the best of yogins—having been consecrated according to the proper order starting from the vows of a lay devotee (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) and so forth—should propitiate the true guru with offerings of pledge substances (*samaya-dravya*) and signs (*saṃketa*). Then, at midnight, having received the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), you must fully measure out the great bliss of the fourth joy (*caturthānanda*) in such a way that it becomes firm.

It says, "Lui speaks," and so forth. Having questioned the glorious Guru regarding the means of the syllabic bliss arising from the union of the vajra and the lotus, you should know day and night the great bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), which consists in the non-perception of all phenomena through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader within the state of *viramānanda*.
And likewise, in the *Śrīsamāja*: "Without the Vajra-Guru, one cannot attain the state of Nirvāṇa, which is the pacification of all afflictions and is irreversible."

And so it has been said by the venerable Nāgārjuna in the *Vajrajāpa*: "Though someone might leap from the summit of the king of mountains, he would not wish for his own fall; yet he nonetheless falls. Likewise, though one who has received beneficial instruction through the grace of the Guru may not desire liberation, he is nonetheless liberated."

In the *Caryāgītikoṣa*, the venerable Saraha also said in his *Prabandha*: "That mind which, through its own causal activity, constructs the wheel of saṃsāra—may that mind, by the grace of him whose sovereignty is beyond conceptual proliferation, bestow upon me its own ground. And may that bliss which arises as a web of conceptual constructions be realized within oneself; one should always place the two feet of that Guru, who is liberated from them, upon one's head with humility."
Also in the Śrī Hevajra: "It is known by oneself through merit and by attending upon the Guru at the [appropriate] times. ||0||

[2] Illuminating the benefits by means of another verse, he says "all meditative absorptions" (*sarvasamādhi*) and so forth. By the Blessed One himself, through various methods, infinite and boundless meditative absorptions have been taught for the sake of abandoning the ten unwholesome actions and for the restraint of the sense faculties. By means of those meditative absorptions, in the method of Great Passion (*mahārāganaya*), nothing at all is accomplished through the difficult observances of the *poṣadha* and other such rules, because they are devoid of bliss.

Therefore, in the *Śrīsamāja*: "By means of difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes miserable; for from suffering the mind is distracted, and through distraction, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is otherwise [prevented]. Likewise, in the *Śrīhevajra*: "The world is bound by passion, and by passion alone it is liberated. This is indeed a 'reversal-cultivation' (*viparītabhāvanā*), which is not understood by the Buddhist outsiders (*buddhatīrthika*). Thus, due to the impairment of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—that is, being devoid of great bliss—the Buddhist outsiders experience many sufferings and undergo birth and death.

They do not share in that [attainment]. And thus the scripture says: "Those devoid of reality do not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of eons. Because of this statement, he also speaks of the practice of the method of Great Passion (*mahārāga*). As it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*: "Having abandoned the five objects of desire, one should not afflict oneself with austerities; one should accomplish awakening with ease, in accordance with the Yoga Tantra."

And so it was said by Saraha-pāda: "If the sprout of the mind, which is extremely delicate, is not watered by the pure juices of the sense objects, how can it attain the state of a wish-fulfilling tree that pervades the sky and bestows fruit?"

The *Caryāgītikopa* [3]: This direct authority, which is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the meaning of the practice of the method of Great Passion, speaks the third word—beginning with "ityādi"—in order to shatter the dogmatic adherence of others who are fixated on false knowledge. Having abandoned the subsequent sounds, the *auḍiyāna-karaṇa*, and so forth, as well as bondage, embrace that which is near—the noose of the dharma of selflessness (*nairātmya*), namely the side of emptiness (*śūnyatāpakṣaka*). "Re" is a vocative address.

O Bhau, those whose nature is liberation! And thus says the scripture: "These are those lofty peaks situated upon the vast mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); when the self is split open by the vajra that awakens to selflessness (*nairātmya*), it undergoes dissolution along with the mountains of innate suffering."
With the fourth line, beginning with "he says" (*bhaṇai*), he speaks of having gained direct experiential conviction (*dṛṣṭapratyayatā*) regarding the greatness of the Dharma as it truly is.

"The Master" (*ādi*) refers to the Siddhācārya Lūyīpāda; he speaks thus: "By me, Lūyīpāda, the Siddhācārya, through the power of meditation—that is, by means of the mental consciousness which has transcended the cycle of sense objects and faculties—through the practice obtained from the fourth instruction received from the Guru, the form of the 'yoked pair' (*yuganaddha*) was seen."
And thus says the scripture: "The senses, as it were, sleep; the mind, as it were, enters within; the body appears as if devoid of movement, swooning in true bliss."

Washing is performed with *āli* through the purification of the moon; rinsing is performed with *kāli* through the purification of the sun. Having established the seat by means of both of these, and being seated with the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*) of one's own deity, it is directly realized.
And so it is stated in the *Dvikalpa*: "The union of *āli* and *kāli* is the throne of Vajrasattva. Thus.

The mother donkey does not know how to carry her young;
she eats the *tentali* fruit of the tree and the *kumbhīra*.
Listen, O neighbor, householder, and friend!
The thief has stolen the blue lower garment. (Chorus: *Ghra dha pada*)
The wine has fallen asleep, the banyan tree is awake;
the thief Kāneṭa asks, "Where has Nila gone? (Dhruva).
By day the *bahur̤ī* tree withers, yet its leaves tremble; by night it becomes *kāmarūpa*. (Dhruva)
In the Āisana-caryā, the Kukkurī-pāda [says]:
"Among millions of goats, one alone is remembered in the heart."
In the Treasury of Dohā Songs: The tortoise cannot hold the milk-pot or the stool;
the crocodile devours the tamarind tree.
"O sir, listen to this petition regarding what has occurred in the courtyard of the house: at midnight, my ear-ornament was stolen."
The mother-in-law has fallen asleep, while the young bride remains awake;
her ear-ornament was carried off by a thief—what course of action does she seek?
During the day, the young bride fears the crows; at night, when the spirits appear, she assumes a form according to her desire.
Such a practice was sung by Kukkurīpāda; it has entered the heart of but one person in the midst of ten million.

With minds delighted by drinking the nectar of their own bliss, Kukkurīpāda spoke in *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language) to reveal that very King of Great Bliss, beginning with the word *dulī*. One should understand that *dulī* refers to the lotus of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in which the dual aspect has dissolved; it is to be understood through the *sandhyābhāṣā*. Due to the context of the *karmamudrā*, its "milking" occurs by way of the sequence of joys (*ānanda*) and so forth; that is the conventional bodhicitta. Having traveled via the *avadhūtī* path, its falling into the *vajramaṇi* at the seat (*pīṭhaka*) is the "holding. It does not go [outward]; immature yogins are not capable of holding it.

And so says Kṛṣṇācāryapāda: "This is that Mount Meru, the supporter of the earth; one cannot cross over its even and uneven heights. Kṛṣṇa says: it is difficult to perceive, difficult to traverse; who can comprehend it with the mind? Therefore, the lords of yogis born from the lineage of the gurus [know that] that very *bodhicitta* is the fruit of the tree of the body, like the fruit of the *ciñcā* tree, though it is crooked.

By means of the kumbhīra [meditation], which is the kumbhaka-samādhi purified by its unique characteristics, and through the sequence of their own direct experience, practitioners effect its consumption— that is, they render it devoid of intrinsic nature.
Strengthening [the argument] with a firm step, he says:
"The courtyard" (aṅganam) should be understood as the wind of emergence and the entry into the house of creative imagination;
"it shines forth" (vibhāti).

Having resolved upon the form of the utterly pure *avadhūtī* within oneself, the Lord of Yogins says: "O you who are the utterly pure *avadhūtī*, listen! First, by means of the instruction on the *vajra*-recitation, lead both [the winds] into the house of the *viramānanda-avadhūtī*.

Then, in that house, at midnight during the fourth junction (*saṃdhyā*), [the state] beginning with 'kāneṭa'—that very abundance of the faults of the winds from the entry and so forth—is stolen by the thief of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)."
The *Caryāgītikoṣa* explains that very same meaning with its second line: "That one who is Sureśvara... and so forth.

Having led the breath of Tvaritā and the others into the fourth bliss (*caturthānanda*) which is the yogic sleep (*yoganidrā*), and having shaken off the conceptual constructions of beginningless existence through the twilight of the term *avadhūtī*, the yoginīs also remain awake day and night in the form of the naturally pure *avadhūtī*.

When the fault of the winds, such as entering [the wrong channels], has been removed by the thief of the radiant light (*prabhāsvara*) of Kāneṭa, then, in the absence of anything to be grasped and so forth, the lords of yogins do not pray for anything whatsoever in the ten directions.
With the third line, he states the benefit of the two truths through the differentiation of the completely pure *avadhūtī*: "During the days," and so forth.

Due to the differentiation of the soft and other levels of intention, that *avadhūtī* conventionally manifests the three worlds in the form of semen; then, having produced the consciousness of day after day herself, she becomes terrified and frightened by the "Kāu" (the person of the time of the body).
And thus says the scripture: "Just as a painter [creates] the form of a yakṣa that is extremely terrifying..."
Having painted it himself, he is indeed terrified; for so is the ignorant one in saṃsāra.
"Rā" means that by means of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), one consecrates the five aggregates and so forth as the naturally pure *avadhūtī*; "kāmarū" means that one proceeds oneself,
without conceptual construction, to the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) within the wheel of one's own abode.

And thus says the scripture: "The innate wind, established in its own state, free from the web of conceptual construction, peaceful and of the nature of emptiness, produces an indescribable satisfaction.

Therefore, through the cause of the many compassionate methods bestowed by the Guru, one who possesses the essence of eternal bliss is empowered to perform deeds for the sake of sentient beings in this unimpeded saṃsāra."
To demonstrate its extreme rarity, he states the fourth line:
"Such is this"—meaning such a practice that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the state and conduct of the Lord of Yogins, which was taught by Kukkurīpāda himself.
Its meaning is that even among millions of yogis, it resides in the heart of but a single yogi.
And so Kṛṣṇācāryapāda says: "One carries the pride of the world, thinking, 'I am an expert in the ultimate truth'; yet among millions, there might be one who is free from attachment."

Having made the *vāruṇī* firm within the innate (*sahaja*), one becomes visibly ageless and immortal when firmly bound. (Jhuṣapada)
On the tenth day, the signs at the door appeared;
the guest came to his own home.
The six-fold deception is spread abroad; the hunter is within, and there is no escape. (Dhruva)
Taking a single lotus with its stalk intact, they say, "O brave one, hold it steady! (Dhruva)
The Treasury of Songs on Conduct: That one liquor-seller connects two houses with smooth bark and binds the *vāruṇī* wine.
Having stabilized it through the innate [state] and joined it with the watery [element], one becomes free from old age and death, possessing firm shoulders.
Having observed the signs from the tenth door, the expansion bestowed within the sixty-four ghaṭikās has entered; indeed, the reciter does not depart. ||3||
A single ghaṭikā is a subtle stalk; having made it firm, move it as it pierces through. 4.

By way of its complete purity, Virūpāda—his mind overflowing with supreme compassion—has spoken to reveal that *avadhūtikā* without doubt, beginning with the words "the single *śuṇḍinī*" and so forth.

Being singular due to its union at the six paths, that *avadhūtikā* is the *śuṇḍinī*, the upper nose. The moon and sun, the left and right [channels], are two powerful ones; the mature yogi causes them to meet and enter into the noble middle channel.
By this, he further solidifies his own self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

Having returned himself, he brings the *bodhicitta*—the drop (*bindu*)—into the cavity at the peak of the *vajramaṇi* below the nose. Through the guru’s instruction, he focuses it with the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), which is free from the stains of ignorance, the seeds of [defilements], and aversion. Because it is the joy of bliss, he binds the *bodhicitta*, [calling it] *vāruṇī*.

With the first line, firming the ultimate *bodhicitta*, he says: "By means of the *sahaja* [joy]," which refers to stabilizing the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) through the cessation-joy (*viramānanda*) by the grace of the Vajra Guru. O child-yogi, "the wine" (*vāruṇī*)—spoken in this esoteric terminology—is that very conventional *bodhicitta* which is to be understood.

Having bound that *bodhicitta*, once it has entered its own empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), with the noose of unchanging bliss (*akṣaratāsukha*), perform that specific practice by which you shall attain the state of being ageless and immortal, with firm limbs.
And likewise, in the *Yogaratnamālā*: "Firm, essential, without flaw, characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible, neither burning nor perishable—emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called the vajra."
They provide a further explanation of this with the words "the tenth," and so forth.

Even at the door of Vairocana, having seen the sign of joy and delight— the treasury of songs on the practice of great passion— the Gandharva-being himself arrives, enters through that door, and gratifies his own mind by drinking the nectar of the lotus of great bliss.
And so Kṛṣṇācāryapāda says: "Behold, the lotus has blossomed; O bee, smell the fragrant nectar! Kṛṣṇa says: "The mind does not depart by any means. (14)
"O wind, blow! The mistress of the house is staying in the home.
Just as there is internal inclusion by means of the self, so it is also from the *sukhavajra*.
This is because of the statement: "He becomes the divider of the self, the grasper of the self, the conqueror of the self, and the lord of the self."
With the third line, he speaks of the cessation of the movement of the gandharva-being:
"sixty-four ghaṭīs," and so forth. By "sixty-four ghaṭīs" is meant "in sixty-four [units] of purification"; this is in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (esoteric language) for the *saṃyogacakra*.
"Ghaḍi" is, in the sandhyā-bhāṣā, that very seat (*āsana*).
There, the *gandharva-sattva* enters into the fire ignited by great passion (*mahārāga*);
its purification does not occur through the wind (*pavana*).
Kṛṣṇācāryapāda says: "It does not go downward, nor does it go upward;
leaving the *veṇī*, it remains motionless."
Kāṇha says: "The mind does not break open by any means; it remains motionless like the wife of the wind in her house. (16) 17 And so he speaks with the fourth line:
"One *ghaḍulī*, etc.

She herself, the previously mentioned *avadhūlī*, is called *ghaṭī* because she brings together (*ghaṭati*) the two truths—conventional and ultimate—and is subtle in form due to the cessation of the two appearances.
Those of the Virūpā lineage speak thus.
By means of that channel of semen (*śukranāḍikā*), following the Guru’s instruction, stabilize that non-fallen *bodhicitta* and move it in a waveless form.

Thus, in the *Sekoddeśa*: "As long as the flow of the cool-rayed moon, consisting of clear light, does not fall into the lotus-petal of the Goddess, having become of one taste with the hosts of Victors;
[then] know that innate form of the All-Pervading Lord—the mountain of compassionate wisdom roaring and piercing the forest of the world with compassion from the tip of the throbbing vajra. (3)
"I shall transform"—thus [thinks] the one who is not [bound by] passion; the lotus-like feet of the sages are like a wound from redness.
The *tiaḍḍā* dance posture is for the sake of the Joraṇi deity; it is a short time.
The nose is vast, like a lotus, a thunderbolt, and a bell.
Without you, my beloved, I cannot live for even a moment; therefore, I shall kiss your face and drink the nectar of your lotus-like mouth.
Pluck out the eyebrows! The union with the void cannot be known;
it is hidden within the lineage of the jewel (maṇikula) at Or̤iyāna.

having kissed your face, I drink the nectar of the lotus.

rend asunder the wings of both the sun and the moon! 3.
Guṇḍarī says: "I am a hero in the *kundura* (the union of the two organs);
among men and women, my loincloth is raised high. ||4||
In the *Caryāgītikāṣa*, the venerable Guṇḍarīpāda establishes that very same meaning—that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature—by means of the practice of Śrī Heruka.
He says, "The *tiya* (*ḍā*)," and so forth;
by this, the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtikā* are meant.
Having caused [the vital energy] to enter the *trinābhi* and rendered it free from appearances, she herself is the utterly pure *Abadhūtikā*, the selfless Yoginī.
Regarding the term *Aṅkavālī*:
she gives her own mark (*aṅka*) as a sign to the practitioner.
And he protects him;
or else, through the application of characteristics such as the variegated (*vicitra*) and so forth, he bestows the sequence beginning with bliss (*ānanda*).
Furthermore, because of the speaker’s unremitting application, he grants consolation.
"Lotus and vajra" means,
O best of yogis, that upon the surface of the perfect union of the vajra and the lotus, there is the state of a mass of bliss (*ānanda*).

Realize the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is free from time.
Therefore, this practitioner, greedy for great bliss, speaks thus:
"O Nairātmyā Yoginī, without you, I am not capable of sustaining the vital winds for even a single moment, because their force is so difficult to restrain and so fickle.
And so says the scripture: "In the states of arising, abiding, and ceasing, there is the persistence of the intermediate state."
Whatever conceptualization exists in the world is the manifestation of wind and mind.

Having kissed your mouth, which is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), I shall, according to the oral tradition of the Guru, at the moment of the *viramānanda* [joy], take the nectar of the lotus—the honey-intoxication of the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, which is the ultimate bodhicitta.
Thus it is said in the Śrī Hevajra: "The unworthy is called the *ḍiṇḍima*; the worthy is considered the *kāliñjara*."
With another verse, he describes the benefit of the Yoginī, beginning with "khepa" and so forth.

Through "projection" (*kṣepāt*), that Yoginī Nairātmyā, who is of the nature of *bodhicitta*, becomes free from the stains of delusion by means of the root of the jewel (*maṇimūla*) through a bliss purified by its distinct characteristics. Furthermore, having experienced the flavor of play therein, she ascends from the root of the jewel and enters into the Great Wheel of Bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Therefore, it was stated by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya: "This is that supreme mountain described by me; this is that state of great bliss.
In a single night, one attains for a moment the innate great bliss."
With the third line, he speaks of complete purification:

*sāsu ghare*, and so forth. First, the Lord of Yogins (Yoga-indra), having preceded this with the yoga of the deity, makes the Body-Vajra firm; then, by means of the instruction on Vajra-recitation, he shatters the seizing of the fortnights (*pakṣagraha*) of the moon and sun, and stabilizes the Speech-Vajra. To make the Mind-Vajra firm, he leads the breath—the abode of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), which has become one in playful union (*ekalaulībhāva*) with innate bliss (*sahajānanda*)—to the peak of Mount Sumeru, the "house" (*āgāra*). This is what is meant by *kuśvikai*.
One should block the entrance at the base of the jewel with the hollowed palms joined like cymbals; then, awakening oneself, one speaks in due order.
And so says the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya: "Just as a firm bolt is placed on the door for the passage of the wind, so too, if the mind is fixed upon the jewel in that terrible darkness."
The Jina says that even if one were to touch the highest heaven (ambara), if one experiences worldly existence (bhava), one attains perfection (sijjhāi) even in nirvāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa says: "While experiencing existence, one attains nirvāṇa."
The accomplished master Guṇḍarī himself proclaimed the benefits through the realization of the vajra-like samādhi,
saying "Speak," and so forth.

Among other yogis who are turned away from the oral tradition, I am the Hero because I crush the afflictions by means of *kundura*— the yoga of the union of the two organs and the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
Furthermore,

among them, "bark garment" (*cīra*) is mentioned as a sign of a master of yoga (*yogindra*), extracted here for the purpose of demonstrating the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), such as the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*).
The Treasury of Songs on Conduct (Caryāgītikoṣa), in the Rāga Gurjarī, by Cāṭilla-pāda: O Ocean, in Your profound current, I am carried away;
having reached the end of one shore, I find no standing place in the midst.

Someone or other may speak ill of you, O Virūpa, but the world of wise men does not abandon your neck. ||3||
Kṛṣṇa sings of you, O Caṇḍālī, O Ḍombī; there is no one else who eats you, O Chiṇṇāṇī. ||4||

To explain that very same meaning for the sake of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through the understanding of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya sets it forth by means of the *ḍombī-sandhyā* (the secret code of the ḍombī):
"The three," and so forth. By me, Kṛṣṇācārya, through attachment to the Vajra Woman, the three worlds—body, speech, and mind—[are realized].
His hundred and sixty natural defects were overcome with ease;
for this very reason, it is said that he "slept," meaning he had entered into yogic sleep (yoganidrā) through his divine play (līlā).
Because of the realization of the selflessness of phenomena.
By means of the phrase "the treasury of the various vehicles" (*vayāgātikoṣa*), he leads those who have not yet attained purification to the state of manifestation;
by what method? And so forth.

"O *bhārbharibhālikā*, O *ḍombinī*, do not falsely impute [this] to me, you who are an impure *avadhūtī*. Having done what? You have caused that which is the *prabhāsvara* (luminosity), dissolved within the body, to be afflicted at the end by the essence of ignorance.
Thinking, 'I shall protect the *saṃvṛti-bodhicitta* (conventional bodhicitta),' you have established the *cittavajra* (mind-vajra) of the *kāpālika*."
By means of another specific word, he further clarifies that very point with the passage beginning "Who indeed... and so forth;
by that *ḍombinī*, through the act of purchasing impure ash, the entire triple world—including gods, asuras, humans, and others—has been "crushed," meaning destroyed, by false knowledge.
Precisely because the hare-holder—the conventional *bodhicitta* that serves as the cause of the clear light—is "struck down" (*ṭālita*) by the yoginī of non-transmission, meaning it is destroyed;
and thus the *Caryāpādas* state: "First, one should destroy the camphor in the mouth," and so forth.
With the third line, beginning with "keho," he describes the true nature of the Ḍombī:

even those who are ignorant of her true nature and do not know you, the Ḍombī, who are the supreme purity of innate bliss (sahajānanda), they too— driven by the power of karma and due to experiencing the sufferings of saṃsāra— speak against you.

Those regional lords of yogis who perceive you through the imperishable bliss of the perfect union of the vajra and the lotus do not, even for a moment day or night, abandon the *saṃbhoga-cakra* at the throat.

Thus says the scripture: "Some yogis, wherever they may be, are eternal connoisseurs of dwelling in the abode of the *pretas*; they possess *kunduru* [sandalwood] throbbing with bliss through the union of the *kakkola* and *priyabola*; their hands are cherished by freshly cleansed rice; they are *cakriṇas* [holders of the wheel] whose lips are devoured by the intoxication of the divine lotus-vessel from which the nectar flows."

With the fourth line, he states the benefit of the Yoginī, beginning with "kāha" and so forth: such a Caṇḍālī, who is the means for accomplishing the rites, is praised as supreme by the Kṛṣṇācāryas, and not by others.
Apart from the Ḍombī, there exists no other woman with a flattened nose, whether she be a courtesan or otherwise;
for, having encountered a particular being, she effects a distinction based on that difference.
And so it is said in the *Jñānasambodhi*: "The mind alone is the great seed of both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa."
In the conventional, it goes toward the conventional; in nirvāṇa, it goes toward the absence of intrinsic nature. ||0||18||
When the sound of the drum resounded, who set out for the wedding of the *ḍombī*? (Chorus)
The Dombī was married; at that very moment she was carried away, and her dowry was brought to her home.
Day and night, attachment to pleasure arose; through the net of the yoginī, night turned into dawn.
The yogi who is enamored with the company of the *ḍombī* does not abandon his natural state, for he is intoxicated.
The mind and the vital breath are two cymbals, while existence and nirvana are the large drum and the hand-drum; these are the musical instruments of the treasury of songs. ||1||
The sound of victory-drum beats has surged forth;
Kṛṣṇa has set out for the wedding of the Ḍombī. ||0||
He married a Ḍombī; his birth was thus brought about, and he established the unsurpassed Dharma—or the unsurpassed abode—through his union. ||2||
Day and night, the yoginī assembly remains engaged in the practice of sexual union; thus, the night becomes dawn. ||3||
The yogi who is attached to the company of the Ḍombī and does not abandon her for even a moment is one who is naturally intoxicated [with the innate joy]. ||4||
The *ḍombī* is that very channel of semen (*śukranāḍikā*), the impure *avadhūtī*; for the purpose of breaking through its obstruction.
When,

having taken the departure-gate of that [state] to be the marriage, and having destroyed the defects such as arising by means of the "victory" (jaya), I, Kṛṣṇācārya, have thereby realized the unsurpassed Dharma through the dowry (yautaka) without effort.
The third line, *vayāgīvikoṣaḥ*, describes the power of the Yoginī.

Regarding the phrase *aharniśaśriyā* and so forth: when the lord of yogins (*yogīndra*) is together with the Knowledge-Seal (*jñānamudrā*), he becomes constantly absorbed in sexual union day and night. By his radiant light, which is the desire of the *koṇī* (the Yoginī), the darkness of the afflictions (*kleśāndhakāra*) flees. And so forth.

And thus says the scripture: "When the Lord, the Master who is superior to the vital breaths, has dissolved into the Self; when the multitude of inhalations and exhalations has ceased and the life-wind has been stilled and restrained—that most radiant expansion of light belonging to the lords of yogis, having emerged from their own very bodies, pervades the three worlds, dispelling all darkness."
[4] With the fourth line, they describe the conduct of the lord of yogins through the grace of the Yoginī,
beginning with "Ḍombī" and so forth:
Ḍombī is that very *avadhūtī*, pure by nature and luminous, who is the *jñānamudrā*.

Because of her attachment to *surata* (sexual bliss), those yogins who are devoted to her do not abandon her for even a moment, since she is the vessel for the bliss of great joy (*mahāsukha*) that bears the head of gnosis (*jñāna*).
Thus, Saraha-pāda says: "When the mind has reached the state of total non-existence... and so forth. ||0||19||
The *Caryāgītikopa*:
[A Song by the Yogin, in the Rāga Paṭamañjarī, by Kukkurīpāda] Hā~u! My hope has vanished; it is equal to the infinite expanse. The delusion of mine cannot be described.
[1] O Mother, my inner fortress has crumbled. That which was sought here is not here at all. (Chorus)
First, know my state of exile; while examining the channels (nāḍīs), it is like a search for a father. 2.
That youth which has not yet filled my heart, O father, you have dug up by the roots and buried in the dust. 3.
Kukkurīpā says: O you who remain in this world, whoever understands this here is a hero. 4.
I am a master of my own mind, free from desires; my state of liberation cannot be described. ||1||
O Mother, having seen that inner chamber, I perceive that whatever I see here is not truly here.
First, my vessel of latent impressions was born; through the investigation of the channels, even that wretched thing was scorched. ||2||
My father has dug up the very root from here, that full-blown youth which was mine. (3)
Kukkurīpāda says: This existence is stable; he who awakens to this here is a hero. ||4||

The *Varyāgītikoṣa* [1]: Kukkuripāda, nourished by drinking the nectar of the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, speaks of that very same meaning within himself, having resolved upon the Blessed Lady Nairātmā-yoginī: *hā~u nirāsī* and so forth. "I am the Blessed Lady Nairātmā, free from hope (*nirāśī*), devoid of attachment (*āsaṃga*). *Khamaṇa* means the mind, which is entirely empty, is the master. In its absorption in *surata* (bliss), there is for me no experience of the excellence of the unchanging union (*akṣara-saṃyoga*); it cannot be made known to anyone through speech. And thus Saraha-pāda says: "Who will understand? To whom shall I speak today? Even if I were to speak, what would be the use? O beloved one, by seeing you, this manifest cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) has been destroyed. [16] By the refrain (*dhruvapada*), he confirms that very same meaning: *phiṭale* and so forth. Therefore, "end" (*anta*) means the limit. Having seen my own little hut, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), [he says] "clearly" (*sphuṭam*): at that moment, the entire host of sense objects and the like was cut down by me, Nairātmā. Addressing himself, he says: "O Mother Nairātmā, whatever enemy of sense objects I see here now, not even one of them exists, because everything consists of great bliss. [2]

With the second line, he states the nature of the investigation, beginning with "In the first," and so forth: At the outset, this body was produced within the vessel of the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). When one investigates this body—its thirty-two channels being the goddesses—in accordance with the sequence of the *piṇḍīkrama* and by the authority of the words of the true guru, how can that wretched latent tendency exist? It simply does not exist at all; rather, it is transcended. [3]

With the third line, beginning with *navayauvana*, he states the fruit of practice. "Root" (*mūla*) refers to the conventional bodhicitta; its "cutting" (*nikṛtti*) was performed at the base of the jewel (*maṇimūla*), within the jewel, by Kukkuripāda through the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*). And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*: "The two banks would be the bell. For that reason, you have brought about the withdrawal of the mandala of sense objects, which is "fresh youth" (*navayauvana*). By the power of that, you have become a beautiful consort for the body of the Great Vajradhara, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. "O Kāyavajra, well done!"—this is said, addressing oneself directly. [4] *Varyāṇīkoṣa*.

With the fourth line, he speaks of the state of direct realization (*sākṣātkāritva*), beginning with "bhaṇathī" and so forth. This worldly existence (*bhava*) is indeed caused by the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). It is "firm" (*sthira*); that is, it is made firm by the lotus-like hands of the lords of yogins (*yogīndra*), who have realized it in its stainless form (*nirañjana-rūpa*) within this mandala. Because they investigate it through knowledge (*vidyā*), they are heroes (*vīra*). And thus says Kṛṣṇācāryapāda: "That which is understood by the rare few in the moment of the innate (*sahaja-kṣaṇa*)" and so forth. [This is the commentary on the twenty-second verse.]
The Treasury of Verses on Various Rāgas: The Rāga Varār̤ī by Bhusuku-pāda. At night, [the world] is like a thief out of fear; nectar is consumed as food by thieves.
Māra is indeed the root that has grown, by which the dense forest of sins is not severed. (Chorus)
The drops of worldly existence have been completely wiped away; the flickering, false, and hollow notions have perished. (Dhruva)
The dark clouds rise up; they do not rain. They lift their hands in the sky to drink the nectar. (Chorus)
Then Mūsā said: "I am unsteady; O True Guru, awaken me so that I may become steadfast. (Dhruva-pada)
When the conduct of Mūsā is broken, Bhusuku says that then the bondage will snap. (Dhruva)
The Treasury of Verses on Various Topics: In the night, which is full of darkness, the mouse acts; having consumed nectar, the mouse makes its meal.
Kill, O yogin, the mouse-like breath, by which the coming and going of the fool does not cease.
The rat that tears through existence digs its way toward a state of rebirth; having swallowed the unstable rat, the Destroyer stands ready to seize either one's stability or one's deposit.
Time is the rat; its color is not [fixed]. Rising into the sky, it drinks the nectar of immortality.
At that time, that mouse is leaping and moving about; through the awakening of a true guru, make it steady.
When the behavior of the mouse falters, Bhusuku says that the bondage perishes.

The *Varyāgītikoṣa* [explains that Bhusuku-pāda establishes this very meaning through the "rat-sandhyā" (secret) terminology: "In the night, the blind one," and so forth. Because it "steals" (*muṣṇāti*), it is called a "rat" (*mūṣaka*). By way of secret terminology, the "mind-wind" (*cittapavana*) is to be understood. "In the night" (*nisi*) refers to Wisdom (*prajñā*), which is to be understood by means of the "hunter" (*kaṅgin*). Through the various moments such as the "wonderful" (*vicitra*) and others, by way of the activity of physical bliss (*kāyānanda*) and so forth, during the union of the *vajra* and the *lotus*, the consumption of the food of the nectar of *bodhicitta*—that very "rat," the mind-wind, performs this itself. At that moment of the "bliss of cessation" (*viramānanda*), by means of the method obtained from the mouth of the venerable Guru, its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is swiftly realized. For the immature yogin who performs this, the coming and going within the wheel of cyclic existence (*saṃsāracakra*) in its dual form does not cease, and the mind does not shine. Thus says the *Āgama*: "In the sky of intense passion, filled with powerful essence, beautiful with the clear perception of skillful renunciation, marked by dense bliss, and where peace is accumulated through various forms within; there this triple world appears in the mind as if it has gone to dissolution. [With the second line, the activity of the "rat-mind" is described: "Existence" (*bhava*), etc. Because it "exists" (*bhavati*), it tears apart its own effect, "existence" (*bhava*), due to its natural fickleness; this very "rat of the mind" brings about a state of alteration. "Goes" (*gati*) means it itself produces the fall into miserable states such as the animal realm and the hells. Therefore, having perceived the natural defect of the rat-mind, O Yogin, you shall not perform the imposition of existence upon it through the instructions obtained by the grace of the Guru. [With the third line, he states its true nature: "Time" (*kāla*), etc. Because it destroys the moon of the conventional *bodhicitta*, that very rat of the mind is "Time" (*Kāla*). Through the analytical investigation of the division of its "lump" (*piṇḍa-prāha*), O Yogin, no instruction for perceiving color exists. "Counting" (*gaṇana*) means: having gone to the lotus-forest of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) according to the Guru's tradition, and returning again, one tastes the drinking of the honey of the mind of ultimate reality. And thus, in another system, the Lord of Fishes (*Mīnamātha*) said: "The Guru speaks of the path of ultimate reality; action is the deer, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the door. ]
The lotus has blossomed; tell me, will the bees not drink the nectar of the lotus? They will certainly not die from fear.

[With the fourth line, he speaks of the greatness of the Vajra Guru: "That," and so forth. This mind-monkey remains puffed up with delusion and pride only so long as it does not encounter the trap for deceiving the true Guru;
therefore, O yogin, let the vow toward the Guru be undertaken.]
And so Saraha-pāda says: "By whose rays of grace," and so forth.

[With the fifth line, he describes the true nature of the rat of the mind (*cittamūṣaka*). "When," and so forth. At the moment when the activity of the rat of the innate bliss-mind (*sahajānanda-cittamūṣaka*)—the superimposition of "I"—is severed, at that moment its bondage to *saṃsāra* is shattered. Thus says the scripture: "In reality, there is no *saṃsāra* for embodied beings; what is the concern regarding bondage? Where there is no bondage for anyone, likewise, for one who is liberated, there is no act of liberation."

The delusion of a snake, a shadow, or a demon in a rope is produced by false superimposition; therefore, abandon nothing, grasp at nothing, and sport as one who is healthy and established in the true state. — *Caryāgītikoṣa*
[Rāgaguñjarī of Saraha-pāda: One who does not abandon the world, but instead creates it through one's own mental constructions, binds oneself with one's own hands.
O inconceivable yogi, do not think that we do not know how death occurs within the cycle of existence.
The state of death is just like the state of life;
there is no difference between them in terms of impurity. Whatever [impurity] exists here in life and in death, let that be applied to the longing for the essence of the essence.
Those gods who wander among the moving and the unmoving are not at all free from old age and death.
What desire is there for one who has abandoned desire?

That which Saraha speaks of is the inconceivable realm. The world, having repeatedly fashioned both cyclic existence and nirvana through the self, falsely binds the self. We do not know [this], O inconceivable Yogin.
What is the nature of the existence of birth and death?
As is birth, so too is death;

there is no difference between living and dying. He who is free from fear regarding birth and death in this world—what need would he have for elixirs or alchemical potions? Those who wander through the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile...

They are neither free from old age nor immortal. (4) Is birth the cause of action, or is action the cause of birth? Saraha says that its abode is inconceivable; it is either that [nature] or Dharma. (5) Saraha-pāda establishes this very point through the realization of all dharmas, beginning with the words "apaṇa" and so forth.

Having engaged in the superimposition of the conceptualization of cyclic existence and nirvana due to the fault of beginningless ignorance and habitual tendencies, this world, through its own delusion, becomes bound by the fetters of existence.
With the verse beginning with "dhruvapadena," the Siddha-ācārya Saraha-pāda himself speaks thus, strengthening his own realization: "amhe" and so forth.

By the grace of the dust of the Guru’s feet, through the thorough knowledge of the true nature of reality (*bhāva-svarūpa*), we yogins are inconceivable; therefore, we do not know what kind of arising, abiding, and destruction occur.
Thus, the venerable single verse [states]: "Free from the defects of arising, abiding, and destruction," and so forth.
In the second line of the *Varyāgītikoṣa*, they state the nature of arising: "Of what [is there arising]," and so forth;
since all things are realized to be selfless (*nairātmya*), for whom does arising exist?
"O lords of yogins," thus addressing themselves, they say:
"For that which has no arising, no destruction is seen.
And so it is stated in the *Advayasiddhi*: "That whose nature neither arises nor perishes is not seen at all."
That knowledge is called non-dual, being entirely free from all conceptual constructions.
Therefore, for a living person, there is no perception of a difference from the deceased;
likewise, it is said: "In the case of one who has slept and awakened, one who desires the fruits of a dream should not conceive of any difference [between them]."
With the third line, they state the benefit for themselves:

"Even that yogi in whom there exists fear of death and so forth might perform various ritual applications of elixirs (*rasāyana*); we, however, are free from fear and beyond conceptual construction regarding the danger of death and the like."
Furthermore, with the fourth line, they state its benefit:
"Those who," and so forth.

Whosoever are yogins in their youth who wander through the great region of Jambudvīpa, including all things mobile and immobile, or who go to the abode of the thirty gods (Tridaśa) by the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like—even they do not attain immortality because they have not obtained [it] through the path of the Guru.
With the fifth quarter, they describe the greatness of the path, beginning with "jām" and so forth:
for the lord of yogis who is devoid of both agent and action, what purpose is served by birth or by action, or even by rebirth?
Therefore, the venerable Saraha expresses his own intention:
"For the yogins who know the ultimate truth are indeed inconceivable. ||0||22||
[The commentary on the twenty-second Caryāgīti] || The Treasury of Caryā Songs ||23||
If you go to the forest of Bhusuku and kill the five people, you will become one-minded while resting in the lotus grove.
[1] Bhela lives, having destroyed the night of ignorance; Bhusuku, without grasping at meat, has entered the lotus grove of the Supreme Reality.
Alas, what a pity! A web of illusion has spread, binding the deer-like mother; who can describe how they are awakened by the instruction of the True Guru?
[2] Bhra || A Treasury of Verses on Conduct: When you go to the monastery named Bhuyuka, you will enter the Makinī grove of Mañcalatā trees; there you shall become single-minded. 1.
One born lives without measure; when dead, there is only a corpse.
Without grasping meat, one enters the lotus forest like a musuku bird. ||0||
Having spread the net of illusion, O friend, the deer of illusion was bound by the True Guru; now that it has been awakened, whose story is for whom? ||2||

Taking the body as the self-vessel, with the earth as the mother, water as the food, and relying on both time and non-time, move the mind along the path of the wind by means of the boat of yoga-measure. ||3|| In the absence of nets, chains, and ropes, the deer flees swiftly;
leaping again and again, it runs through the midst of the sky without sound, until the night of the fool's feet becomes dawn. ||4||

With his heart impelled by that very same innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the venerable Bhūṣukapāda elucidates this very point for the sake of spiritual accomplishment through the *hariṇasaṃdhyā* [language]:
"If you... and so forth.

O Bhūṣuka! If you—[meaning] if your body-wind (*kāyapavana*) has the nature of the body-wind of a deer (*hariṇakāyapavana*)—then, having performed the practice of the conduct (*cārikākṛtya*) directed toward the methods for making [all things] devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvakaraṇa*), [you shall attain success].

Then, within the five sense objects, the aggregates, and the elements—such as the earth element, the eye faculty, and so forth—one should first perform the activity of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) through the sequence of the mandala clusters. Subsequently, by means of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*), having suppressed that [conceptual] vision with the syllable *HŪṂ*, one enters the great bliss wheel (*mahāsukhacakra*) through the union of the vajra and lotus by the grace of the Guru. "Hohisi ekumanā" signifies the state free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
[Thus] he awakens himself, who was formless.
Dhru: To confirm that meaning, he speaks of the purity of the support (*ālambana-śuddhi*) with the word *dhruva* (the fixed), beginning with "they live" (*jīvante*).
When the breath enters, the syllable *oṃ* is the life-force (*jīva*), which is daytime-consciousness endowed with forty inherent natures.
When the breath has departed, the dead corpse is the syllable *A-HŪṂ*, which possesses the nature of the thirty-three [deities] and is the knowledge of night;
the root of the abiding breath is the syllable *BHĀ*, which possesses the nature of the seven [deities].
Likewise, Vajrapāṇi also said: "By means of the syllable OṂ, those who desire bliss enter the refuge and are protected by the supreme."
Emitting sentient beings with the syllable *hūṃ*, they abide in the syllable *ā*.
The treasury of the various lineages (*varyāgotikoṣa*) likewise states the transcendence [of the stages] beginning with "the vision during the night-watch" and so forth.

Having caused the knowledge of the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) and the rest to enter the middle channel, and thereafter [having consumed] "flesh"— which in the sandhyā-bhāṣā refers to the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) whose nature is the self-perfected state (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)— one must not, O Bhūsukapāda, fail to enter the abode of great bliss (*mahāsukhagṛha*) by means of the fourth bliss (*caturthānanda*).
Likewise, in the *Pañcakrama* it is said: "It does not exist at night, nor in the twilight, and it is not found even by day," and so forth;
and in the same way, Saraha-pāda also says: "Wherein the sense-faculties set, and wherein one does not abide in intrinsic nature."
"O, ask about that innate bliss at the feet of the Guru.
With the second line, beginning with "māyājāla," he states the means for the path.
One should conceive of "māyā" as a limb of ritual action; having superimposed it as a web whose effect is the mass of bliss obtained in the various moments [of the ritual],
one should bind the deer of the body with it and, through the grace of the Guru's feet, cause its entry into the midst of its own nature.
For that purpose, at that time, the realization of the nature of the experience of bliss cannot be described in any way whatsoever;
and thus, the venerable Saraha also stated: "The worlds are delighted by bliss," and so forth. 3.
With the third line, he states a specific aspect of cultivation:
"The body is the vessel for the self," and so forth;
for the body indeed constitutes the fourfold vessel of the self.
From that, the five great elements arise as objects to be consumed;

therein, the moon and sun represent the proper and improper times. Thirdly, in the *avadhūtī*, for the sake of destroying all obstacles through the fourth bliss (*caturthānanda*), one should render food and drink devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
And likewise, in the *Śrīkālacakra* it is said: "When the semen-drop is retained or falls, day and night," and so forth.
With the fourth line, beginning with "jāla-ṣṭṛ-kha-la," he speaks of the attainment of the fruit.

In this context, the "net" (*jāla*) of great bliss and supreme joy is to be understood as "bodily bliss" (*kāyānanda*) according to the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*); the "chain" (*śrṅkhalā*) is to be understood as "vocal bliss" (*vāgānanda*) according to the intentional language;
and the "rope" (*rajju*) is to be understood as "mental bliss" (*cittānanda*).
All that, including form and so forth, is to be seen as empty;
this is the descent into luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Thus, this deer of a body, whose nature is wind,
having fled,
becomes devoid of intrinsic nature; the yogi who has practiced constantly dissolves into the luminosity of space.
For that purpose, by the venerable Bhusuka, "the night" (*rajanī*)—meaning the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*)—is said to have been "driven away" (*dūrita*), which means it has fled.

Likewise, from the *Āgama*: "In that very same way, the Lord, the Sovereign of Life, remains dissolved," and so forth. [End of verse 23. Now, the *Taryāmīvikoṣa* [verse 24]: [In the *Rāga Indratāla*, by the venerable Kṛṣṇācārya:
"When the full moon rises..."
Then the king of the mind becomes stainless.
The impurity of delusion is severed by the teacher’s instruction;
the sense-objects and the senses have entered the sky. (Chorus) The seed-syllable equal to space merges into that which is equal to space.
The tree of the self plants its seed in the mind within the three realms;
just as when the sun has risen, the night departs, so too the dust of delusion in the ocean of existence is cast far away.
Just as a royal swan distinguishes the water, the foot of Kṛṣṇa says, "Enjoy worldly existence. When the full moon appears, it shines. 4. May he manifest.

The King of Great Bliss (*mahāsukharāja*), whose essence is the relish of all phenomena as objects of focus—that Kṛṣṇācārya—further contemplates that very same meaning in the verse beginning with "the full moon" (*pūrṇacandra*). By the grace of the Guru, when the sixteen-faceted lunar disc of the *bodhicitta* arises, then the King of Wealth (*vittarāja*) of the Lord of Yogins becomes utterly stainless.
